items.title: A friend or neighbour asks about a claim (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Data Protection Act 2018; department guidance
items.body: Civil servants who work with benefits, tax, immigration or other personal records will be asked from time to time by friends, relatives or neighbours to look at a case. The rules are clear and apply whatever the grade. You may only access a person's record when your job requires it. Looking at the record of someone you know, even to help them or out of concern, is unauthorised access. It can be a breach of the Data Protection Act 2018, and in some cases a criminal offence. Departments monitor who looks at records, and unauthorised access leads to disciplinary action, which can include dismissal. The right response is polite and firm. Explain that you cannot look at or discuss anyone's case outside your official duties, and tell the person how they can get help themselves, for example by contacting the department through its normal channels or using the online account. If you already hold a record because it is part of your work, you still must not pass details to anyone who is not the customer or an authorised representative. If the person is a relative or close friend and their case lands in your work queue, tell your manager as it is a conflict of interest, and the case should be passed to someone else. If you are ever unsure whether you can look at something, stop and ask your manager before you act. Remember too that the duty of confidentiality applies in conversations in the pub or on social media, not just at work.

questions.prompt: Your neighbour says her benefit payment is late and asks you to check it on the system. What should you do?

options.text: Explain that you cannot look at her case and suggest she contacts the department
Ask a colleague to check it and let you know the answer
Look at the case but tell her nothing about what you see
Check it quickly and tell her only whether or not the payment is on its way to her account

questions.hint: Looking at a neighbour's case without a work reason is unauthorised access.

questions.prompt: A relative's claim appears in your work queue. What is the correct action?

options.text: Process it carefully, because you know the details of the case very well
Tell your manager so that the case can be given to someone else
Leave it in the queue until another colleague picks it up
Process it but ask a colleague to check your work afterwards

questions.hint: A relative's claim is a conflict of interest and must be declared.

questions.prompt: A friend who is the customer's cousin phones and asks you to confirm the amount of a payment. The customer is not on the call. What do you do?

options.text: Give the amount, since the cousin is part of the family and already knows about the claim
Give a rough figure so as not to reveal the exact amount
Tell the cousin to ask the customer to call back later and share nothing else
Decline to give details and explain only the customer or a representative can discuss it

questions.hint: Details can only be given to the customer or an authorised representative.

questions.prompt: What can happen to a civil servant who looks at a record without a work reason?

options.text: A small fine paid to the Information Commissioner
A warning that is removed after one week
A request to complete a short online course only
Disciplinary action, which can include dismissal

questions.hint: Departments monitor access and take it seriously.

questions.prompt: Which statement about looking at a friend's record to be helpful is correct?

options.text: It is allowed if you do not change anything
It is allowed if the friend gives you permission verbally
It is allowed in your lunch break
It is still unauthorised access even if you mean well

questions.hint: Good intentions do not make access authorised.

questions.prompt: You are in a pub and a friend asks you about a high-profile case you worked on. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them what you can once they promise not to repeat it
Say you cannot discuss your work and change the subject
Tell them only the details already reported in the press
Share the outline but leave out any names

questions.hint: Confidentiality applies outside work too.

questions.prompt: How can you help a friend who has a problem with their claim without breaking the rules?

options.text: Tell them how to contact the department or use their online account
Ask a colleague in another team to deal with it for you as a favour to your friend
Look at it after work hours so that nobody notices
Pass them a copy of the guidance on the claim

questions.hint: Signposting is allowed; accessing records is not.

questions.prompt: You are unsure whether you may look at a file. What is the right step?

options.text: Stop and ask your manager before you act
Ask a friend in another department for their view
Look at it and report afterwards if there was a problem
Check whether the file shows who last looked at it

questions.hint: Ask first if you are unsure.

items.title: Gifts, favours and pressure from suppliers (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; department gifts and hospitality policy
items.body: Civil servants who deal with suppliers, contractors or customers must be careful with offers of gifts, hospitality and favours. The Civil Service Code requires staff to avoid anything that might be seen to influence their judgement. In practice, departments set limits and require recording. Typical rules say that small gifts of low value, such as a calendar or a few chocolates from a customer, may be accepted openly and recorded. Larger items must be declined. Cash, vouchers and any gift from a supplier who is bidding for work or who has just won a contract must be declined or reported. Hospitality such as a working lunch connected to a meeting may be fine if it is modest and approved by a manager, while tickets to sporting or cultural events, or an invitation to a lavish dinner, usually need a manager's approval or must be declined. Offers made to your family also count. If an offer is made to you, thank the person politely, explain the department's rules and decline if in doubt, then tell your manager and enter it in the register. A favour can also be an offer of a job interview, discount or a lift that comes with an expectation of something in return. If someone hints that a gift would be linked to a decision, report it at once, because it may be an attempt at bribery. Bribery is a criminal offence under the Bribery Act 2010, and an attempt should be reported to your manager and the department's counter-fraud team.

questions.prompt: A supplier waiting for a contract decision invites you to a free weekend at a hotel. What should you do?

options.text: Accept as long as you do not influence the decision
Accept if you pay for your own meals
Decline, tell your manager and record the offer
Accept and tell your manager once you have returned

questions.hint: Offers from bidders must be declined and recorded.

questions.prompt: A customer leaves you a small box of chocolates after you resolved a long-running problem. What is the best action?

options.text: Return them by post with a formal letter
Keep them for yourself, because it is a personal thank-you for your own work
Tell your manager and follow the department's rules on small gifts
Accept them only if nobody else is watching

questions.hint: Small gifts are handled openly according to the policy.

questions.prompt: A supplier hints that you will get a discount on a holiday if the contract goes their way. What should you do?

options.text: Tell the supplier you will think about it
Report it at once to your manager and the counter-fraud team
Mention it to a colleague over coffee
Ignore the hint and decide the contract strictly on its merits

questions.hint: This may be an attempt at bribery.

questions.prompt: Which law makes bribery a criminal offence?

options.text: The Official Secrets Act 1989
The Equality Act 2010
The Bribery Act 2010
The Data Protection Act 2018

questions.hint: The Bribery Act 2010 covers bribery.

questions.prompt: A supplier offers your sister a job interview just after your department awards them a contract. What should you do?

options.text: Encourage your sister to apply, because it is a very good opportunity for her
Tell your manager because it could be seen as a reward for the contract
Accept on her behalf and say nothing
Ask the supplier to wait until after the contract is signed

questions.hint: Offers to family count and could appear to influence judgement.

questions.prompt: A modest working lunch is provided at a meeting you were asked to attend by your manager. What is the usual rule?

options.text: It is allowed only for senior staff
It must always be refused, whatever the value or the circumstances
It may be acceptable if modest and linked to the meeting
It is allowed only if it is paid in cash

questions.hint: Modest hospitality linked to work may be fine.

questions.prompt: What should you do after declining an offer of a gift?

options.text: Tell the supplier's manager about your decision only
Pass it to a colleague to deal with
Forget about it because nothing was accepted
Tell your manager and record it in the register

questions.hint: Declined offers are still recorded.

questions.prompt: Why are vouchers treated like cash?

options.text: They are subject to tax
They can be exchanged for goods and so are easily misused
They are not allowed by most suppliers who deal with the government
They are not legal tender

questions.hint: Vouchers carry the same risk as cash.

items.title: Spotting and handling mistakes at work (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; department quality assurance guidance
items.body: Everyone makes mistakes, and the Civil Service expects staff to own up quickly, put things right and learn. The Civil Service Code says civil servants must correct any errors as soon as they become aware of them. A culture in which people hide mistakes is dangerous because small errors grow and customers can be harmed. If you realise you have made a mistake, first stop and avoid making it worse. Then tell your line manager or team leader straight away, explaining what happened, when you noticed it and what you think the effect is. Together you can decide how to put things right: for example, correcting a record, stopping a payment, or contacting the customer to apologise and explain. Keep a clear note of what happened. If you notice a colleague's mistake, tell them politely first, or tell the team leader if it is serious or if the colleague is not available. Do not ignore it, and do not correct it in secret, because the manager needs to know about patterns. Mistakes that involve personal data, such as sending a letter to the wrong address, must be reported straight away through the department's incident process, because there are legal reporting deadlines. In most cases, reporting quickly is treated sympathetically, while hiding a mistake is treated seriously. Checking your work, using checklists and asking when unsure all help to prevent errors.

questions.prompt: You realise you have typed the wrong bank details onto a customer's payment. What do you do first?

options.text: Email the customer to ask for the correct details yourself
Correct the details quietly and hope that nobody notices
Tell your team leader straight away and explain what happened
Wait to see whether the payment goes out before saying anything

questions.hint: Mistakes must be reported promptly so they can be put right.

questions.prompt: A colleague regularly enters the wrong date on forms. What is the best step?

options.text: Tell other colleagues so that they check the forms too
Mention it politely to them and tell the team leader if it continues
Wait for the quality checks to pick it up in the end
Quietly correct each form yourself without ever telling anyone about it

questions.hint: Raising a pattern helps prevent harm to customers.

questions.prompt: A letter containing a customer's details has gone to the wrong address. What should you do?

options.text: Report it at once through the department's incident process
Ask the customer to contact the person who received it
Write a note in the file and take no further action
Wait for the wrong recipient to post the letter back to the department

questions.hint: Data incidents have legal reporting deadlines.

questions.prompt: Why are small mistakes dangerous if they are hidden?

options.text: They can grow, and customers can be harmed before anyone notices
They are always a criminal offence under the Code
They are counted against the whole team's bonus
They always cost the department a very large amount of public money

questions.hint: Hidden errors tend to grow.

questions.prompt: How are mistakes that are reported quickly usually treated?

options.text: As grounds for dismissal during your probation
As a reason to reduce your pay for the month
As serious misconduct that is recorded permanently on your file
Sympathetically, with a focus on putting things right

questions.hint: Quick reporting is encouraged.

questions.prompt: Which habit helps prevent errors in your work?

options.text: Using a checklist and checking your own work before it is passed on
Skipping breaks so that you can finish more cases
Working much faster at the end of the day so that you meet your targets
Avoiding questions so that you appear confident

questions.hint: Checking and checklists reduce mistakes.

questions.prompt: Why should you not correct a colleague's mistake in secret?

options.text: Colleagues usually prefer to correct their own work
It wastes time that could be spent on your own cases
The manager needs to know about patterns and risks
It is against the law to alter another person's work

questions.hint: Managers need to see patterns to put things right.

questions.prompt: What should you tell your manager when you report a mistake?

options.text: What happened, when you noticed it and what the effect may be
Only the name of the customer who is affected
Only the time at which the mistake took place
Your view on which colleague is most to blame for what went wrong

questions.hint: A clear account helps to put things right.

items.title: Working with social media and the press (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service social media guidance; GOV.UK
items.body: Civil servants have the same right to personal opinions as anyone else, but their role means they must take care online and when dealing with journalists. The Civil Service Code and department social media guidance say that staff should not post anything that could damage trust in their impartiality, reveal official information or bring the department into disrepute. Examples are criticising ministers or government policy, posting partisan political comments, sharing photos of the workplace that show confidential material, and posting details of casework. Even if your profile is private, posts can be copied and shared. Do not say you are speaking for your department unless you are authorised. Treat colleagues and customers with respect online, because abusive posts or bullying are disciplinary matters. If someone contacts you from the press, the rule is that you do not give your own comments or information. Politely say you are not the right person, and pass the enquiry to the department's press office, who handle all media contact. Do not confirm or deny anything. This applies even if the journalist seems to know a lot, or if they are a friend. If you come across a post by someone else that reveals official information, tell your manager. If you think something is wrong in your workplace, use the Code's route for raising concerns rather than social media, because going public first can break confidentiality rules and may weaken your legal protection.

questions.prompt: A journalist rings your office and asks about a case that is in the news. What should you do?

options.text: Confirm the facts that have already been reported in public
Tell them to call back when your manager is in the office
Say you are not the right person and pass the enquiry to the press office
Give a short comment as long as you avoid mentioning any details of the case

questions.hint: The press office handles all media enquiries.

questions.prompt: Which online post would put your impartiality in doubt?

options.text: Posting a photograph of a weekend walk with your family
Sharing a recipe with friends in a private group
Criticising the government's policy on a public forum
Congratulating a friend on starting a new job

questions.hint: One-sided political comments undermine trust in impartiality.

questions.prompt: You are unhappy about a decision at work. What is the Code's route for raising it?

options.text: Discuss it in a public group that other staff belong to
Raise it with your manager or the nominated officer first
Tell a journalist so that the matter is properly investigated
Post about it anonymously on a public forum to get attention

questions.hint: Internal routes come first.

questions.prompt: Why can a private social media profile still be a risk?

options.text: Ministers are able to see private posts of staff
The department can read every private profile
Private profiles are not allowed for civil servants
Posts can be copied and shared by other people

questions.hint: Private posts can still spread.

questions.prompt: You see a colleague's public post showing a confidential document on their desk. What should you do?

options.text: Tell your manager so that the matter can be dealt with
Ignore it because it is on their own account
Reply to the post in public to tell them to remove it at once
Share the post with other colleagues to warn them

questions.hint: Possible disclosures should be reported.

questions.prompt: When may you say you are speaking for your department online?

options.text: Whenever you work in a communications team
Whenever you mention your job in a post
Only when you have been authorised to do so
Whenever you add a note saying the views are your own

questions.hint: Authorisation is needed to speak for the department.

questions.prompt: A journalist friend asks about an unannounced decision and says it is off the record. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them the details if they promise not to name you
Decline to comment and refer them to the press office
Give a hint without confirming the full details
Say you cannot say, but that they are on the right lines

questions.hint: Friendship does not change the rule.

questions.prompt: What is the likely effect of going to the press before using the internal routes?

options.text: It may break confidentiality rules and weaken legal protection
It is required by the Civil Service Code in urgent cases
It will guarantee that you remain anonymous
It will speed up the investigation into your concern considerably

questions.hint: The proper routes should be used first.

items.title: What to do when asked to do something you think is wrong (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
items.body: Most of the time, instructions at work are reasonable, but occasionally a civil servant may be asked to do something that seems wrong, such as to alter a record, ignore a rule, favour a friend or hide a mistake. The Civil Service Code covers this. If you are asked to act in a way that you believe is illegal, improper, unethical, or in breach of constitutional convention or professional standards, or if you are being required to act in a way that is inconsistent with the Code, you should report it to your line manager or another manager, or to the nominated officer. Before you act, try to be calm and clear about what concerns you. You can ask for the instruction to be confirmed in writing. Write a note of what was said, when and by whom, and do not do the thing you believe is wrong. Sometimes the matter is a misunderstanding, and asking for clarification resolves it. If you are still not satisfied after the department has responded, you may take it to the Civil Service Commission. Evidence of criminal activity should be reported to the police or the appropriate authority. A person who raises a concern properly and in good faith is protected from victimisation by the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998. Do not discuss the concern with colleagues who might be involved, and do not take away documents you are not entitled to take. Raising a concern is a duty of public service, and it is a mark of integrity.

questions.prompt: Your supervisor asks you to change the date on a record so a deadline looks as if it was met. What should you do?

options.text: Make the change this once, but refuse if it is asked again
Ask a colleague to make the change instead of you
Make the change but keep a copy of the original record for your own protection
Decline and raise it with another manager or the nominated officer

questions.hint: Altering a record to mislead breaks honesty.

questions.prompt: You are given a verbal instruction that you believe is wrong. What is a sensible first step?

options.text: Refuse in front of colleagues so that they hear
Ignore it for now and wait to see whether it is repeated
Ask for the instruction to be confirmed in writing
Carry it out and say nothing about your concerns

questions.hint: Writing it down makes the position clear.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you avoid when you have a concern about wrongdoing?

options.text: Reporting it to a manager in the department
Discussing it with colleagues who might be involved
Keeping a note of what was said, when it was said and by whom
Asking the nominated officer for advice

questions.hint: You should not tip off people who may be involved.

questions.prompt: Why might you ask for clarification before reporting a concern?

options.text: It may turn out to be a misunderstanding that can be put right
It improves your chances of promotion
It allows you to avoid the Civil Service Code
It prevents the matter from being recorded anywhere in the department

questions.hint: Clarification can resolve some concerns.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you to skip a check for a friend of the department's director. What do you do?

options.text: Explain the check applies to everyone and raise it if pressed
Skip it and tell a colleague what you did
Skip the check this once to avoid an argument with your manager
Do a shorter version of the check instead

questions.hint: Rules apply equally to everyone.

questions.prompt: Which law protects a person who raises a concern properly and in good faith?

options.text: The Data Protection Act 2018
The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
The Equality Act 2010 and its public sector duty
The Freedom of Information Act 2000

questions.hint: The Public Interest Disclosure Act protects whistleblowers.

questions.prompt: You find proof that a colleague has stolen money. What should you do?

options.text: Wait for the next audit to discover it
Confront the colleague privately and ask them to pay it all back
Report it to your manager and, if appropriate, the police
Take the evidence home to keep it safe

questions.hint: Criminal activity must be reported.

questions.prompt: Why is raising a concern a mark of integrity?

options.text: It puts the duty of public service above personal comfort
It protects you from any later disciplinary action
It shows that you disagree with the decisions of your managers
It is the quickest way to win a promotion

questions.hint: Integrity means public duty comes first.

items.title: The election period and a change of government (level 5)
items.source: Cabinet Office, Guidance on the Conduct of Civil Servants; Civil Service Code; Cabinet Manual
items.body: A general election changes the government but not the Civil Service. In the weeks before polling day, there is a pre-election period, sometimes called purdah. During it, departments avoid announcing new policies or making major decisions that would commit a future government, and avoid using public resources in a way that could appear to help one party. Government business continues, services keep running, and civil servants carry on with their normal work, including paying benefits and processing claims. Civil servants must be extra careful not to do anything that suggests support for one party, such as sharing political content on work systems. Ministers remain in office until a new government is formed, and civil servants continue to serve them. Before an election the Cabinet Secretary may allow the civil service to give opposition parties information to prepare for office, with the agreement of the Prime Minister. After the election, the Civil Service gives the same level of help and advice to the new government as to the old one. New ministers get briefings about the department and its work, and civil servants advise on how to put manifesto commitments into practice. Civil servants do not comment on whether policies are good or bad, but advise on practicalities, cost and legality. If a hung Parliament follows, civil servants help ministers while the position becomes clear, but do not take part in negotiations between parties. A change of government is therefore a normal part of the job, and one that civil servants are trained to handle.

questions.prompt: What is the pre-election period often called?

options.text: Recess
Dissolution
Prorogation
Purdah

questions.hint: Purdah is the informal name for the pre-election period.

questions.prompt: During the pre-election period, what happens to services such as paying benefits?

options.text: They are paid by the Electoral Commission
They are reduced to the most urgent payments only
They are paused until the new government starts
They carry on as normal

questions.hint: Public services continue.

questions.prompt: A new government takes office. How should civil servants treat the new ministers?

options.text: Ask them to confirm their policies before offering advice
Give them the same help and advice as the previous ministers
Wait to see whether they win a second term
Give them less help until they have proved themselves in office

questions.hint: Civil servants serve each government equally.

questions.prompt: Why do departments avoid announcing major new policies in the pre-election period?

options.text: Because ministers are banned from entering their offices
Because it is a criminal offence for a department to announce policies
Because the Civil Service closes during elections
To avoid tying a future government's hands or favouring a party

questions.hint: Purdah protects the fairness of the election.

questions.prompt: A new minister asks what you think of a manifesto commitment. What is the right approach for a civil servant?

options.text: Pass the question on to the Opposition's office
Refuse to give any advice about manifesto policies
Say whether you personally think the policy is a good idea or a bad one
Advise on practicalities, cost and legality without judging the policy

questions.hint: Advice should be impartial.

questions.prompt: What happens to civil servants after an election that produces a hung Parliament?

options.text: They join in the negotiations between the political parties as advisers
They stop work until the new government is chosen
They choose which party will form the next government
They help ministers in office but stay out of party negotiations

questions.hint: They stay impartial.

questions.prompt: Which of these should you avoid during the election period?

options.text: Discussing the weather with colleagues
Voting in the election in the same way as any other citizen
Using work systems to share political content
Carrying on with your usual casework

questions.hint: Work systems are not for party politics.

questions.prompt: Who stays in office until a new government is formed?

options.text: The most senior civil servants in each department
The Cabinet Secretary
The Leader of the Opposition
The existing ministers

questions.hint: Ministers stay until a replacement government is in place.

items.title: Which organisation deals with what? (level 5)
items.source: GOV.UK, Departments, agencies and public bodies
items.body: Part of serving the public well is knowing where to send people when their enquiry is not for you. Here are some common examples. For tax, including Income Tax, National Insurance contributions, tax codes and Child Benefit, people contact HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC). For benefits such as Universal Credit, Pension Credit, Attendance Allowance, Personal Independence Payment and the State Pension, people contact the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), which has Jobcentre Plus for people looking for work and the Pension Service. For driving licences and vehicle tax, they contact the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA), and for driving tests, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA). For passports, they contact HM Passport Office, and for visas and immigration, UK Visas and Immigration, which is part of the Home Office. For court matters in England and Wales, they contact HM Courts and Tribunals Service (HMCTS), and for prisons and probation, HM Prison and Probation Service. Company registrations go to Companies House, and land and property ownership to HM Land Registry. Complaints about the NHS in England go to the NHS complaints process first, and then the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman. GOV.UK has pages for each of these, and the website is the best place to send people for accurate, up-to-date information. When you signpost, be clear about which organisation to contact and, if you can, how. Do not guess.

questions.prompt: A caller wants to renew their driving licence. Where do you direct them?

options.text: The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency
HM Revenue and Customs
The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency
HM Passport Office

questions.hint: The DVLA issues and renews licences.

questions.prompt: A caller asks about the State Pension. Which department deals with it?

options.text: HM Revenue and Customs, which also pays some benefits
The Department for Work and Pensions
The Ministry of Justice
The Home Office

questions.hint: DWP handles the State Pension.

questions.prompt: A caller wants to book a practical driving test. Which body runs driving tests?

options.text: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency
The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency
The Department for Transport's press office
HM Passport Office

questions.hint: The DVSA runs driving tests.

questions.prompt: A caller asks about their tax code. Who should they contact?

options.text: HM Revenue and Customs
The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency
HM Treasury
The Department for Work and Pensions

questions.hint: HMRC deals with tax codes.

questions.prompt: A caller needs to apply for a visa to visit the UK. Where should they be directed?

options.text: HM Revenue and Customs
UK Visas and Immigration, part of the Home Office
The Department for Work and Pensions
HM Passport Office, which also sits within the Home Office

questions.hint: UKVI deals with visas.

questions.prompt: A caller wants to find out who owns a plot of land in England. Who keeps these records?

options.text: HM Courts and Tribunals Service
The Department for Transport
Companies House
HM Land Registry

questions.hint: HM Land Registry records ownership.

questions.prompt: A caller wants to register a limited company. Where should they go?

options.text: The Cabinet Office
HM Land Registry
HM Revenue and Customs
Companies House

questions.hint: Companies House registers companies.

questions.prompt: A caller is unsure which organisation they need. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them it is not a matter for the Civil Service
Tell them to try every department in turn
Check GOV.UK or your guidance rather than guess
Give your best guess in case it is right

questions.hint: Signpost accurately and do not guess.

items.title: Choosing the right job and grade from an advert (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service grades
items.body: When you read an advert, you can use several clues to decide whether a job is right for you. The grade tells you the level: AA or AO for entry roles, EO for a step up. The summary says what the team does, and the main duties list the tasks. The person specification and essential criteria set out what you must be able to show, and these are what the sift is based on. If you cannot meet an essential criterion, for example a required qualification, a nationality rule or a level of security clearance, you will normally be rejected, so check these first. The advert states the assessment methods, such as a personal statement, behaviours, strengths, a test or an interview, and dates for each stage. It also gives the location and working pattern, including whether the job is full time, part time, flexible or hybrid, and the salary range. Look at whether the job is in an agency, department or arm's length body. If you are weighing two jobs, compare them using the facts in the advert: pay, location, duties, grade and chance of progression. Do not choose a job only because it is at a higher grade, since you must be able to show the behaviours at that level. Equally, do not rule yourself out if you meet the essentials but not the desirables. If you need an adjustment, use the contact in the advert early. If a question is not answered in the advert, ask the named contact.

questions.prompt: An advert says a particular security clearance is essential and you do not have it. What is sensible?

options.text: Check whether it can be obtained and, if not, look elsewhere
Apply and say that you will get it after you start
Apply and say that you already hold it
Apply anyway and hope that the requirement will be waived for you

questions.hint: Essential criteria must be met.

questions.prompt: Which part of the advert tells you how you will be assessed?

options.text: The job title and the department's logo
The line that gives the closing date
The section that shows the salary range and the closing date
The section listing the assessment methods and dates

questions.hint: The advert sets out the assessment methods.

questions.prompt: An advert lists desirable criteria you do not meet, but you meet all the essentials. What should you do?

options.text: Not apply because you do not meet every one of the criteria listed
Apply only after you have gained the desirable skills
Apply, since desirable criteria are helpful but not required
Ask the department to remove the desirable criteria

questions.hint: Only the essentials are required.

questions.prompt: Two jobs are both at AO grade. One is full time in your town and the other is part time 40 miles away. What helps you decide?

options.text: Choosing the one that has the shorter and simpler advert to read
Choosing the one whose department you have heard of
Applying to both without reading them closely
Comparing duties, hours, location and travel for your situation

questions.hint: Use the facts in the adverts.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to choose a job only because it is at a higher grade?

options.text: Higher grades are not open to applicants from outside the Civil Service
You must be able to show the behaviours expected at that level
Higher grades are always based in London
Higher grades never offer any training

questions.hint: You will be assessed against that grade.

questions.prompt: Where do you find the closing date and time of a vacancy?

In the advert

items.title: Emails, attachments and sending to the right person (level 5)
items.source: Information Commissioner's Office; department security guidance
items.body: A large share of data breaches in organisations happen because of simple errors such as sending an email to the wrong person, attaching the wrong file, or copying in too many people. Civil servants can reduce the risk with a few habits. Check the recipient's name and email address before you press send, especially when autocomplete suggests a name. Check the attachment is the right one and has no hidden information, for example in other sheets of a spreadsheet. Use the blind copy (Bcc) field when emailing several people who should not see each other's addresses. Do not forward long email chains without checking what is lower down in the thread. Use the department's secure email or file transfer when sending sensitive information, and password protect or encrypt where policy says so. Do not send documents to a personal email account to work at home. Be wary of phishing, which is a fake email that tries to trick you into giving a password or opening a harmful link or attachment. Signs include a sender you do not recognise, a sense of urgency, spelling mistakes, an unexpected attachment, or a link that does not match the website it claims to be from. Do not click. Report it using the department's phishing process. If you do send information to the wrong person, tell your manager and the data protection team straight away, ask the recipient to delete it and not use it, and keep a note of what happened.

questions.prompt: You are about to email a spreadsheet of customers' details to a colleague. What should you do first?

options.text: Check the recipient's address and the attachment is the right file
Send it quickly to meet the deadline
Send a copy to your personal email account as a backup in case of problems
Send it to the whole team to be on the safe side

questions.hint: Checking recipients and files prevents breaches.

questions.prompt: You are emailing several customers about the same matter. How should you address the email?

options.text: Put all the addresses in the To field so each person can reply
Use Bcc so the customers cannot see each other's addresses
Put all the addresses in the Cc field
Send one email and ask them to delete the other addresses

questions.hint: Bcc protects privacy.

questions.prompt: An email says your password will expire in an hour and asks you to click a link. What should you do?

options.text: Forward it to colleagues so that they can check
Click the link and change your password quickly
Not click and report it as a possible phishing email
Reply to the sender to ask whether or not the email is genuine

questions.hint: Phishing should be reported.

questions.prompt: You realise you have sent customer details to the wrong person. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the recipient to ignore it and promise to tell nobody else
Wait to see whether the recipient replies
Tell your manager and the data protection team straight away
Delete your sent email and carry on

questions.hint: Breaches must be reported promptly.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a sign of a phishing email?

options.text: A greeting that uses your name and job title correctly
A message sent by a colleague you know
Urgency and a link that does not match the claimed website
A message written in clear and plain English with no errors

questions.hint: Urgency and mismatched links are common signs.

questions.hint: Hidden content in a thread can cause a breach.

Use department-approved equipment or remote access
Print it and carry it home in your bag
Save it onto a USB stick that you own

questions.hint: Use approved systems only.

questions.hint: Hidden data can be disclosed by mistake.

items.title: Equality in practice: customers and colleagues (level 5)
items.source: Equality Act 2010; Civil Service Code; GOV.UK
items.body: Equality is not only a legal matter, it shows in everyday choices. When you serve customers, give everyone the same standard of service, whatever their age, disability, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or other characteristic. Use respectful language, avoid assumptions and treat each person as an individual. Customers may ask for reasonable adjustments, such as a letter in large print or braille, a call at a particular time, an interpreter, or the help of a trusted person. You should respond to the request, record it and pass it on according to your department's process. Do not ask for unnecessary personal details or make the customer prove their disability beyond what the process requires. Among colleagues, equality means no jokes, comments or behaviour that demean others, and it means supporting colleagues who ask for adjustments, for example a different desk, adjusted hours or software. If you witness discrimination, harassment or bullying, you should challenge it if it is safe to do so and report it to your manager, HR or the nominated officer. Unacceptable behaviour breaks the Civil Service Code and can lead to disciplinary action. Remember that staff may have caring responsibilities, health conditions or faith needs that mean they ask for flexible working. Responding fairly to such requests, within the rules, helps the Civil Service keep good people and serve the public well.

questions.prompt: A customer who is blind asks for letters in braille. What is the right response?

options.text: Send letters as usual with a note for them to ask for help
Ask them to bring a friend or relative with them to read the letters to them
Record the request and pass it on so letters come in braille
Tell them that this is not possible

questions.hint: This is a reasonable adjustment.

questions.prompt: A customer who speaks little English asks for an interpreter. What should you do?

options.text: End the call and ask them to write instead
Follow the department's process for arranging an interpreter
Ask them to bring a relative along to interpret for them on the call
Use simple English only and continue the call

questions.hint: The department arranges appropriate help.

Laugh along with the joke so as to avoid causing a scene in the office
Say nothing because it is not your business

questions.hint: Unacceptable behaviour should be challenged.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks for adjusted hours because of a health condition. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Refer the request to their manager to be considered under the rules
Refuse the request because it would be unfair on the rest of the team
Agree on the spot without telling the manager
Tell the colleague to apply to another department

questions.hint: Requests should be considered properly.

questions.prompt: A customer asks for calls to be made at a set time of day because of a medical condition. What is the best response?

Bullying a colleague

Asking for training to improve your work

questions.hint: Bullying is unacceptable.

questions.hint: Assumptions can lead to unfair treatment.

It is required by every manager in the department
It helps to keep good staff and serve the public well

questions.hint: Fair treatment helps the whole organisation.

items.title: Complaints and difficult conversations (level 5)
items.source: GOV.UK, Complain about a government service; department guidance
items.body: Even in a well-run service, customers sometimes get angry, upset or abusive. How you respond affects the customer's experience and your own wellbeing. Start by staying calm and speaking at a steady pace. Let the person say what they need to say without interrupting, and acknowledge their feelings: for example, I can hear this has been frustrating. Check you understand the problem. Do not argue, take it personally or become defensive. Explain what you can do and what will happen next, and be honest about what you cannot do. If the customer wants to complain, tell them how to do so and record the complaint, rather than trying to talk them out of it. If a call becomes abusive, for example the customer shouts, swears or threatens you, use your department's policy. This usually means giving a clear warning that the call will end if the behaviour continues, and then ending it if it does. Record what was said, then tell your team leader so you can be supported. Never ignore threats. Report them straight away, because they may need to be passed to the police. After a hard call, take a short break, and talk to your manager or use the wellbeing support, such as an employee assistance programme, if you need to. Some customers are vulnerable and their distress comes from ill health, bereavement or money worries, so patience matters. Others may be abusive for no clear reason. In every case, you are expected to treat people with respect, and you are entitled to be treated with respect too.

questions.prompt: A customer shouts that their payment is late and swears at you. What is the first response?

options.text: Raise your voice to match theirs and be firm
Transfer them to another team without explanation
Warn them straight away that you will end the call if they continue
Stay calm, let them speak and acknowledge their frustration

questions.hint: Calm acknowledgement helps de-escalate.

questions.prompt: The customer continues to swear after you have warned them. What should you do?

options.text: Put them on hold for an hour
Carry on with the call for as long as it takes until they finally stop
End the call under the department's policy and tell your team leader
Hang up without saying anything

questions.hint: Follow the department's policy.

questions.prompt: A customer says they want to make a complaint. What is the right response?

options.text: Tell them how to complain and record it

Try to talk them out of making a complaint
Tell them that complaints take months to be answered

questions.hint: Complaints should be recorded and passed on.

questions.prompt: A customer threatens to harm you. What should you do?

options.text: Hang up and say nothing to anyone
Report it at once so it can be passed to the police if needed
Ignore it, because it was probably only said in the heat of anger
Argue back to show you are not frightened

questions.hint: Threats should never be ignored.

questions.prompt: Which phrase acknowledges a customer's feelings?

options.text: That is not my fault and it is not the department's either
I can hear that this has been frustrating for you
I am too busy to discuss this now

questions.hint: Acknowledgement helps to calm a situation.

questions.prompt: After a very difficult call, what is a sensible step?

options.text: Take a day's leave without telling anyone

Take a short break and speak to your manager or wellbeing support

questions.hint: Look after your own wellbeing.

questions.prompt: A customer is distressed because of a bereavement. How should you respond?

options.text: Show extra patience and offer help where you can

questions.hint: Patience matters with vulnerable customers.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of defensive behaviour?

options.text: Arguing that the problem is not the department's fault
Listening to the customer without interrupting them
Offering to help with what you can
Asking questions so that you understand the problem more fully

questions.hint: Defensiveness tends to escalate a situation.

items.title: Protecting information when working away from the office (level 5)
items.body: Many civil servants work at home or in different places some of the time. The security rules still apply wherever you are. Use only department-issued laptops and approved remote systems for official work, and connect through the secure route you have been given. Do not use public wi-fi in cafes or stations for official work unless the department's guidance allows it, because others may be able to see your activity. Do not let family members or friends use your work laptop or phone, and do not discuss work matters where others could overhear, including on phone calls on trains or in public places. Lock your screen whenever you leave your device. Position your screen so that it cannot be read by others. Keep paper to a minimum, and if you must carry paper, keep it in a bag with you, not in a car or left on a train. Return papers to the office for secure disposal, instead of putting them in domestic bins. Report loss or theft of a laptop, phone, pass or papers immediately, even if it happens outside working hours, because quick action can allow a device to be locked or wiped. Do not use personal devices or accounts unless the department has approved this. Voice assistants and smart speakers in your home may be listening, so avoid sensitive conversations near them. Cyber scams can be especially common when working remotely, so be alert to phishing. If you are unsure whether something is allowed, ask your manager or security team before you act.

options.text: Take it in the kitchen while the rest of the family are there

items.title: Starting well: your first month as an AO (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Jobs; GOV.UK, Civil Service Learning
items.body: The first month in a new job shapes how you settle in. In a Civil Service AO role, a good start combines learning the work, building relationships and looking after yourself. Make sure you know who your line manager is, who to ask for help, and who your buddy is if you have one. Learn the rules for hours, breaks, leave and sickness reporting, because these are set by the department and you should follow them, for example by contacting your manager before your start time if you are ill. Complete mandatory learning on time. Ask questions, and check you have understood the guidance for your work. Keep notes of what you learn and ask your manager about anything that you find unclear. When you make a mistake, say so early. Set objectives at your first one-to-one and agree how you will be measured. Build good relationships with colleagues: introduce yourself, be reliable and offer help when you can. Be careful with what you share, as you will see customers' private data from your first week. Take your breaks and look after your health, because the work can be demanding. If you have any concerns about the job or about your own wellbeing, use your one-to-ones to raise them. If you have asked for an adjustment, check that it has been put in place. After a month you will be more confident, so reflect on what you have learned and what help you still need, and note examples you can use later when applying for promotion.

questions.prompt: You wake up ill in your second week and cannot work. What should you do?

options.text: Wait to see whether you feel better in the afternoon
Ask a colleague to pass on a message later
Stay at home to rest and let your manager know on the day you return to work
Contact your manager before your start time, as the department's rules say

questions.hint: Follow the absence procedure.

options.text: Ask the customer how it should be handled
Leave it in the queue for a colleague to do

questions.hint: Report mistakes early.

options.text: Introduce yourself, be reliable and offer help

questions.hint: Being friendly and reliable builds trust.

options.text: They can be used as evidence in later promotion applications

questions.hint: Examples help later.

questions.hint: Raise the problem early.

questions.hint: Look after yourself.

items.title: Outside work, expenses and honest records (level 5)
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; department conduct policy
items.body: The Civil Service Code and department rules cover some parts of life outside the office. Before taking a second job, a paid role as a company director, or an unpaid role such as a trustee or a councillor, you should tell your manager and get approval where your department requires it. The test is whether the outside interest could conflict with your official duties, take too much of your time or energy, or harm the reputation of the department. For example, working part time for a company that bids for government contracts is likely to be a conflict, while a weekend job in a shop usually is not. You should also tell your manager if your personal circumstances change in a way that could affect your work or security status, such as serious debt, because pressure on finances can be a risk for people who handle money or sensitive information. Honest records matter too. Timesheets, flexi records and attendance records must show the hours you worked, and not the hours you were expected to work. Expenses may only be claimed for genuine costs incurred on official business, with receipts where required, and following your department's rules on travel and subsistence. Claiming for a journey you did not make is fraud. Using work time or equipment for private business, such as running your own online shop, is not allowed. Work IT should be used for work, though many departments allow limited personal use in your own time if it does not break security rules. If you notice that a colleague is falsifying records or claims, raise it with your manager or the nominated officer. Being open about these matters protects both you and the department.

questions.prompt: You are offered weekend shifts at a shop. What should you do before accepting?

options.text: Accept, because weekend work in a shop is none of the department's business
Accept, and mention it at your next annual review
Check your department's rules and tell your manager if approval is needed
Accept, and tell your manager only if it affects your attendance

questions.hint: Outside work should be declared where the rules require it.

questions.prompt: A company that regularly bids for your department's contracts offers you part-time work. What is the right response?

options.text: Accept but avoid working on any of their contracts
Tell your manager, because it is likely to be a conflict of interest
Accept as long as you only work for them in the evenings and weekends

questions.prompt: You worked 35 hours this week but the rota says 37. What do you record on your timesheet?

The hours you were expected to work

questions.prompt: Which of these expenses claims is acceptable?

A taxi fare for the journey home from a social event with your colleagues
A meal you bought on a day you were not working
A train fare for a journey made on official business, with a receipt

questions.hint: Only genuine costs on official business may be claimed.

You must not use work time or equipment for your private business
You may use it if your team leader does not mind

questions.hint: Work time and equipment are for official use.

questions.prompt: You notice a colleague claiming expenses for journeys they did not make. What should you do?

questions.hint: Falsifying claims is fraud and should be reported.

questions.prompt: Which of these is likely to need approval before you take it on?

options.text: Playing in a local football team at the weekends
Joining a book club

questions.hint: Directorships can conflict with official duties.
